cards.back: Present it to the nearest SBP-BSC office for authentication before acting on it.

cards.front: Partly notes, partly instruments for travel
cards.back: Prepare two separate T-1 forms showing the amounts released in each form.

cards.question: A customer holds an SBP permit allowing monthly remittances on a non-cumulative basis. Last month she remitted nothing. This month she asks to send two months' worth. What should the dealer do?
options: Send both months, because the permit is still valid
Send only this month's amount, because unused monthly amounts do not carry forward
Send both months if she signs a declaration
Refuse entirely until SBP-BSC reissues the permit
cards.explanation: Under the second type of permit, the monthly limits are not cumulative: an unused balance in one month cannot be carried into later months. Only the cumulative type allows carry-forward within validity.

cards.title: Talking to customers about FX rules
cards.body:
Chapter 2 asks dealers to bring the regulations to customers' notice, and Chapter 10 asks them to warn applicants about false statements. Make that easy:

- Explain **why** a document is needed, not just that it is.
- Never invent a rule. If you are unsure, check with the head office **focal person** instead of guessing, as the call centre did.
- Tell customers that unused exchange must be surrendered to a dealer.
- Keep the website's FX service page current so call-centre staff and customers read the same thing.

cards.title: Hingol case: rewriting the call-centre script
cards.body:
A fictional case from Hingol Bank's files.

After the Manchester fee complaint, Sadia's team listened to 40 recorded calls about education, medical and travel FX. In 11 calls, agents gave wrong or incomplete answers: some said only main branches could help, others quoted documents that the bank's own procedures did not require.

**What changed**
- The call-centre FX script was rewritten with the head office focal person and checked against the bank's Chapter 17 procedures.
- Contact-centre agents joined the branch FX staff in the yearly training-needs assessment, because paragraph 4(ii) names them expressly.
- A short 'which branch can help me?' answer pointed customers to every authorized branch.
- The website page on FX services was updated, as paragraph 4(iv) expects.

Three months later, repeat calls on FX services had fallen sharply and the branch complaint log showed no new 'wrong information' cases.

cards.title: Travel Counter take-aways
items: Offer travel, education and medical FX efficiently at every authorized branch, with a head office focal person and enough notes in stock.
Train every official who serves individuals for FX, including contact and call-centre staff.
Use Form I for imports, T-1 for travel and M for everything else; applications reach SBP only through a dealer.
Approvals last up to 30 days unless stated or revalidated; act only for the original applicant and the named beneficiary.
Foreign exchange must be used for its stated purpose; unused amounts are surrendered to a dealer.

cards.prompt: If a customer called your bank's contact centre tomorrow about sending money for a child's studies abroad, would the answer be right? What would you check or change first?

quiz.question: Under Chapter 2, paragraph 4, where must Authorized Dealers offer foreign exchange services for travel, education and medical treatment abroad?
options: Only at their main branch in each province
Only at branches with a treasury desk
At all their authorized branches
Only through head office, by appointment
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 4(i) asks dealers to ensure these services are offered efficiently by all their authorized branches. Restricting them to main branches is exactly what caused the Manchester fee complaint.

quiz.question: Which outward remittance form covers the sale of foreign exchange for travel?
options: Form I
Form T-1
Form M
Form E
quiz.explanation: Chapter 10 lists three outward remittance forms: Form I for imports, Form T-1 for travel and Form M for all other remittances. Form E belongs to exports.

quiz.question: A student's father applies to remit university fees. The transaction needs SBP's prior approval and is outside the dealer's delegated powers. What does the dealer do?
options: Forward the application to SBP with its comments under stamp and signature
Ask the father to take the form to SBP-BSC himself so the approval reaches SBP more quickly
Approve it anyway because education is a genuine need
Reject it, since dealers cannot handle such cases
quiz.explanation: Where SBP's prior approval is needed, the dealer forwards the application with comments under its stamp and signature. Applications that reach SBP directly from applicants are sent back to be resubmitted through a dealer.

quiz.question: An SBP approval on Form M is dated 33 days ago. It states no longer validity and has not been revalidated. The applicant asks the dealer to remit today. What is correct?
options: The dealer may remit because approvals last 60 days
The dealer should not remit until the approval is revalidated
The dealer may remit if the amount is unchanged
The dealer may remit after taking a fresh declaration from the applicant about the purpose
quiz.explanation: SBP authorizations are valid for a period not exceeding 30 days from approval unless expressly approved for longer or revalidated. Dealers must not remit against lapsed approvals.

quiz.question: A customer asks for a bank draft for an outward remittance even though a telegraphic transfer is available and would cause her no hardship. What does Chapter 10 expect?
options: Issue an uncrossed draft in the beneficiary's name, because the customer's preference governs
Issue a draft payable to bearer to speed up payment
Refuse the remittance until she accepts a cheque
Use a telegraphic or mail transfer, since drafts are for cases of real hardship
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 6 asks dealers to avoid drafts where a telegraphic or mail transfer can be used. Drafts may be issued where the normal transfer would cause hardship, and then must be crossed 'Account Payee only' in the beneficiary's name.

quiz.question: A traveller returns early and has unused foreign exchange bought for the trip. What does Chapter 10 require of him?
options: Keep it in his foreign currency account for his next trip, provided it is within twelve months
Transfer it to a relative travelling abroad
Surrender the unused foreign exchange to an Authorized Dealer immediately
Deposit it with SBP-BSC within 30 days
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 20 requires foreign exchange to be used only for the purpose for which it was obtained. If it cannot be used in full or in part, it should be surrendered to an Authorized Dealer immediately.

quiz.question: Hingol Bank's contact-centre agent tells a caller that medical treatment remittances are handled only at head office. Which Chapter 2 duty has the bank failed to meet in that call?
options: Keeping the public buy-sell margin within 50 paisa per US dollar on every customer quote
Filing returns of FX dealings on their due dates
Sending executives to SBP-BSC meetings when called
Training contact-centre staff in FX business and the rules on individuals' needs
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 4(ii) requires officials serving individuals for FX, including contact and call-centre staff, to be adequately trained and know the rules. The other duties exist but are not what the call shows.

quiz.question: A permit allows monthly remittances on a cumulative basis. The customer remitted nothing in the first two months and now asks to remit those two months plus next month's amount in advance. What may the dealer do?
options: Remit the two unused months plus this month, but not next month's amount in advance
Remit all four months, since the permit is cumulative
Remit only this month's amount, because unused amounts under any monthly permit lapse each month
Remit nothing until SBP-BSC confirms the balance
quiz.explanation: Under the cumulative type, unused amounts for earlier months carry forward within the permit's validity, but remitting ahead of later months' entitlements is not permitted.

quiz.question: A remitter presents a Form M approved by SBP, bearing the serial number of another Authorized Dealer. Hingol Bank agrees to remit. How should Hingol handle the form?
options: Send the remitter back to the other dealer, which alone may act
Remit under the other dealer's serial number without changes
Ask SBP-BSC to cancel the approval and reissue it on a Hingol form, in Hingol's own name, before any remittance is made
Insert its own prefix and serial number from a blank form, score out the other dealer's, and destroy that blank form
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 16 lets a dealer act on another dealer's approved form by inserting its own identifying prefix and serial number from one of its blank forms, scoring out the original under proper authentication and destroying the blank form used.

quiz.question: Which detail does Chapter 2, paragraph 4 give about where the detailed rules on individuals' genuine FX needs are found?
options: They are in Chapter 12 of the Manual
They are in Chapter 17 of the Manual
They are issued only to banks by private letter
They are in the Branchless Banking Regulations
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 4 points to Chapter 17 for the detailed instructions on releasing or remitting foreign exchange for individuals' education, medical treatment, travel and similar needs. Chapter 12 covers exports.

sessions.title: Home Remittances and Proceeds Realization Certificates
sessions.summary: Deliver home remittances the way Chapter 10 requires: credit and payment timelines, the compensation owed for delays and SBP's power to penalise, review of remittance agreements, and the electronic and summary proceeds realization certificates (e-PRC and S-PRC) that staff must be trained to issue and verify.
objectives: Apply the Chapter 10 timelines for crediting or paying home remittances by each delivery route
Calculate the compensation a beneficiary is owed when a home remittance is delayed
Explain the same bank and different bank models for e-PRCs and S-PRCs and who reports the inflow
Describe the staff training, focal person and verifying-agency duties in the e-PRC guidelines

cards.title: Three days late
cards.setting: Home Remittances unit, Hingol Bank head office, Karachi. 10:00 am.

lines.text: A complaint from Riyadh. A driver sent money through our correspondent to his mother's account at another bank in Mardan. It reached her three days after we received the funds.

And a second one from Hyderabad: a nurse in Dubai sends money home every month, and her brother needs proof of the inflow for a government office. Our branch told him to 'come back next week' for a certificate.
I'm Shakeel Ahmed, one of Imran's agents in Mardan. Customers ask me about these certificates every day. I don't know what to tell them.
Two very common failures: speed and paperwork. Chapter 10 covers both, and it puts a price on delay.
Training Lead, this is the Remittance Corridor. By the end you should be able to tell me what we owe the mother in Mardan.

scenes.heading: No restriction on inflows
scenes.narration: Chapter 10 places no restriction on receiving remittances from abroad. Authorized Dealers may freely buy telegraphic and mail transfers, drafts and bills payable in foreign currency.

scenes.heading: A mechanism with deadlines
scenes.narration: To encourage overseas Pakistanis and others to use banking channels, banks must run a mechanism, set out in an SBP payment systems circular of 2009, that credits or pays beneficiaries within fixed times.

scenes.heading: Compensation for delay
scenes.narration: If a remittance is credited or paid late, the beneficiary is entitled to a return for each day of delay at the rate the Manual sets. The bank must pay it.

scenes.heading: Penalties for patterns
scenes.narration: Where SBP sees a tendency to delay, through inspection or the pattern of complaints, it may impose penalties under the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962.

scenes.heading: Agreements reviewed first
scenes.narration: Before finalising home remittance agreements with entities in or outside Pakistan, banks send the drafts to SBP's Exchange Policy Department for input. Responsibility for protecting the bank's interest stays with the bank.

cards.title: The home remittance clock
cards.caption: Chapter 10, paragraph 4(i). The clock starts when the bank receives the funds.

items.label: Same bank account
items.detail: Beneficiary banks with the receiving bank: credit the account at once.

items.label: Other bank account
items.detail: Receiving bank passes intimation and funds to the beneficiary's bank, at most 24 hours after receipt.

items.label: Beneficiary's bank credits
items.detail: Once funds and intimation arrive, the beneficiary's bank credits the account at once.

items.label: Pay order or demand draft
items.detail: Issue and dispatch the instrument within 24 hours of receiving the funds.

items.label: Cash over the counter
items.detail: Where cash payment is offered, the funds must be available at once.

cards.question: A remittance arrives at Hingol Bank for a beneficiary who banks elsewhere. What is the latest Hingol may pass the credit to the beneficiary's bank?
options: Within 24 hours of receiving the funds
Within three working days
By the end of the following week
Whenever the next settlement batch runs
cards.explanation: Paragraph 4(i)(b) requires the recipient bank to intimate and credit the other bank in line with the 2009 payment systems circular, and in any case within 24 hours of receiving the funds. The beneficiary's bank then credits instantly.

items.label: Per PKR 1,000 per day
items.detail: Return owed to the beneficiary for each day a home remittance is credited or paid late.

items.label: Longest normal window
items.detail: Other-bank credits and pay orders or drafts; everything else is instant.

items.label: Worked example
items.detail: PKR 200,000 delayed 3 days: 200 x 0.65 x 3.

items.label: Penalty law
items.detail: SBP may penalise a tendency to delay under the Banking Companies Ordinance.

cards.title: e-PRCs and S-PRCs in brief
cards.body:
A **Proceeds Realization Certificate (PRC)** is documentary proof that funds received from abroad were realized in Pakistan, whether workers' remittances, export proceeds, equity or loans. Dealers issue the **e-PRC** digitally in SBP's standard format with a system-generated unique number, and send an **S-PRC** (summary) at the end of each financial year to every customer issued e-PRCs that year.

**Same bank model.** The beneficiary banks where the funds arrived. That bank emails the certificate to the registered address or posts it on an online portal for the customer to retrieve.

**Different bank model.** The recipient (intermediary) bank sends the money to the beneficiary's bank with complete transaction information in the standard SWIFT MT102/MT103 format. The beneficiary's bank issues the e-PRC and S-PRC. Only the recipient bank reports the inflow in ITRS.

**Cash over the counter.** Ask for an email address if the customer has one. If not, issue and hand over the PRC instantly while paying the rupees.

The old requirement to issue e-PRCs in duplicate has been withdrawn.

cards.title: Who does what with certificates
cards.prompt: Match each situation to what the e-PRC guidelines expect.

pairs.left: Beneficiary banks with the receiving bank
pairs.right: Receiving bank issues the e-PRC by email or through its online portal
Beneficiary's bank issues the e-PRC from the full data the recipient bank sends
Done only by the recipient or intermediary bank

pairs.left: Cash payout, customer has no email
pairs.right: PRC issued and handed over instantly with the rupee payment
S-PRC sent digitally to every customer issued e-PRCs that year
Dealer informs the relevant verifying agencies

cards.title: The different bank model, step by step
cards.prompt: Put the flow of a home remittance and its certificate in order when the beneficiary banks elsewhere.
steps: Funds arrive from abroad at the recipient bank
Recipient bank sends the amount to the beneficiary's bank with complete MT102/MT103-format information
Recipient bank reports the inward remittance in ITRS
Beneficiary's bank credits the beneficiary's account instantly
Beneficiary's bank issues the e-PRC, and later the year-end S-PRC

cards.title: The government office calls
cards.setting: Hingol Bank, Latifabad branch, Hyderabad. 3:30 pm.

lines.text: The nurse's brother is back. A government office says it cannot verify the certificate our branch emailed him because the purpose isn't recorded on its portal.
Our branch staff didn't know we had a focal person for verifying agencies, or that the purpose should be recorded at all.
The guidelines expect dealers to acquaint or train relevant head office and branch staff on issuing and verifying e-PRCs and S-PRCs, so they can guide customers.
So who explains it to people like me at the agent counter?
We do, through training. Let's fix the case first.

cards.title: Cash, no email, needs proof today
cards.situation: A beneficiary collects a home remittance in cash over the counter at an authorized branch. She has no email address and needs proof of the foreign inflow for an official application tomorrow. The cashier suggests she 'come back next week when the certificate is generated'.

choices.text: Issue and hand over the PRC instantly while paying her the rupees, with complete information in the standard format.
choices.outcome: Right. For cash over the counter where the customer has no email, the guidelines require the dealer to issue and hand over the PRC instantly while disbursing the cash.

choices.text: Pay the cash now and email the certificate to a relative's address instead.
choices.outcome: Poor. Sending her certificate to someone else's email is not what the guidelines provide and risks her data. She has no email, so the PRC is handed over on the spot.

choices.text: Pay the cash and tell her to collect the certificate from the beneficiary's bank.
choices.outcome: Poor. In a cash payout the paying dealer is the one issuing the certificate; there is no other bank holding her account.

choices.text: Ask her to wait while the branch requests the certificate from head office, then hand it over later that day.
choices.outcome: Partly right. She would get it, but the guidelines expect instant issue at disbursement, and staff should be trained so no delay is needed.

cards.title: Recipient bank or beneficiary's bank?
cards.prompt: In the different bank model, sort each task to the bank that performs it.

items.text: Receives the funds from abroad
Passes the credit on within 24 hours of receipt
Sends complete transaction data in MT102/MT103 format
Reports the inward remittance in ITRS
Credits the beneficiary's account instantly on receipt
Issues the e-PRC to its account holder
Sends the year-end S-PRC to the customer

cards.back: Sixty-five paisa per thousand rupees per day of delay, paid by the bank to the beneficiary.
Possible under the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962 where inspection or complaints show a tendency to delay.
Drafts go to SBP's Exchange Policy Department before finalising; the bank remains responsible for its own interests.
Each dealer assigns one and shares contact details with verifying agencies.
Dealers arrange with verifying agencies that the purpose of each e-PRC verification is recorded on the portal.
Dealers acquaint or train relevant head office and branch staff on issuing and verifying e-PRCs and S-PRCs.

cards.question: In the different bank model, which bank reports the inward home remittance in ITRS?
options: Both banks, so that SBP can reconcile them
Only the beneficiary's bank, which issues the e-PRC
Only the recipient or intermediary bank
Neither bank; the correspondent abroad reports it
cards.explanation: The e-PRC guidelines say the beneficiary's bank issues the e-PRC and S-PRC, but only the recipient or intermediary bank reports the inflow in ITRS. Double reporting would overstate inflows.

cards.title: Hingol case: paying for the Mardan delay
cards.body:
A fictional case from Hingol Bank's files.

The Riyadh driver's remittance of PKR 300,000 reached Hingol on a Monday morning. The beneficiary's account was at another bank, so Hingol had 24 hours to pass the credit on. A failed batch file was not noticed until Thursday morning, so the credit went three days late.

**Compensation owed:** 300 thousands x 65 paisa x 3 days = PKR 585, paid to the mother without her having to ask.

**Root cause:** a manual hand-off between the SWIFT team and the interbank payments team, with no exception report for unsent credits.

**Fixes**
- An automated alert for any home remittance not passed on within 20 hours.
- A monthly check of delay compensation paid, reviewed by the head of operations, because SBP looks at patterns of complaints.
- A short module on the remittance clock and compensation added to the FX training plan for remittance and branch staff.

cards.title: Remittance Corridor take-aways
items: Same-bank credits, cash payouts and credits by the beneficiary's bank are instant; other-bank credits and pay orders or drafts go within 24 hours of receipt.
Late credit or payment costs 65 paisa per thousand rupees per day, and a pattern of delays can draw SBP penalties.
e-PRCs are issued digitally in a standard format; S-PRCs go to every e-PRC customer at the end of each financial year.
In the different bank model, the beneficiary's bank issues certificates and only the recipient bank reports the inflow in ITRS.
Dealers appoint an e-PRC focal person and must acquaint or train head office and branch staff to issue and verify certificates.

cards.prompt: Pick one home remittance route your branch or unit handles. Where could the 24-hour or instant deadline slip, and how would anyone notice before the customer does?

quiz.question: A home remittance arrives for a beneficiary who keeps her account at the same bank. When must the bank credit it?
options: Within 24 hours
Instantly
By the next working day
Within three working days
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 4(i)(a) of Chapter 10 requires instant credit where the beneficiary's account is with the same bank. The 24-hour window applies only to other-bank credits and to pay orders or drafts.

quiz.question: A home remittance of PKR 100,000 is credited four days late. Using Chapter 10's rate, how much compensation does the beneficiary receive?
options: PKR 260
PKR 65
PKR 400
quiz.explanation: The return is 65 paisa per thousand rupees per day: 100 thousands x 0.65 x 4 days = PKR 260. PKR 65 ignores the days, and PKR 2,600 multiplies by ten in error.

quiz.question: A beneficiary asks for her home remittance by demand draft. What is the bank's deadline?
options: Issue and dispatch the draft within 24 hours of receiving the funds
Issue the draft within a week, when the courier runs
Issue the draft instantly at the time of receipt
Issue the draft within 24 hours of the beneficiary's written request, whenever she makes it
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 4(i)(c) requires pay orders or demand drafts to be issued and dispatched within 24 hours of the bank's receipt of the funds. The clock starts with the funds, not with a later request.

quiz.question: Inspection data shows that Hingol Bank regularly credits home remittances late, and complaints follow the same pattern. Which consequence does Chapter 10 provide for, besides compensation?
options: SBP automatically withdraws the bank's Authorized Dealer licence
The FMU fines the bank under the AML Act
SBP may impose penalties under the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962
The beneficiaries must sue the bank in civil court
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 4(iii) says that where SBP notes a tendency to delay, through inspection or the pattern of complaints, it shall impose penalties under the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962. Licence withdrawal is a separate power, not automatic.

quiz.question: Hingol Bank is about to sign a home remittance agreement with an overseas money transfer partner. What must it do before finalising?
options: Obtain a licence for the overseas partner from SBP's Exchange Policy Department before signing
Send the draft agreement to SBP's Exchange Policy Department for its input
Register the agreement with the Banking Mohtasib
Nothing, because SBP takes responsibility for these agreements
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3 requires banks to forward drafts of all home remittance agreements to the Exchange Policy Department before finalising them. SBP may give input, but responsibility for safeguarding the bank's interest stays with the bank.

quiz.question: A customer whose home remittance landed in his Hingol account asks how he will receive his e-PRC. Which answer fits the same bank model?
options: By email to his registered address, or from Hingol's online issuance portal
From the correspondent bank abroad that sent the money
Only as a paper certificate, issued in duplicate and collected in person from his home branch
From SBP after Hingol reports the inflow in ITRS
quiz.explanation: Under the same bank model, the bank issues the e-PRC to its account holder at the registered email address or uploads it to its online portal. The requirement to issue in duplicate has been withdrawn.

quiz.question: When must an Authorized Dealer send S-PRCs, and to whom?
options: At the end of each financial year, to every customer issued e-PRCs that year
Every month, to all customers who received any home remittance during that month at all
Only when a customer asks for one in writing
At the end of each quarter, to SBP and the customer
quiz.explanation: The guidelines require dealers, at the end of each financial year, to send S-PRCs digitally to all customers who were issued e-PRCs during the year.

quiz.question: A government verifying office tells Hingol it cannot see why an e-PRC was verified on its portal. Which guideline addresses this?
options: Dealers issue every e-PRC in duplicate for the verifying office
Dealers send the certificate to the verifying office by post
Dealers stop issuing e-PRCs to customers who deal with that office until the portal is fixed
Dealers arrange with verifying agencies that the purpose of each verification is recorded
quiz.explanation: The guidelines ask dealers to make the necessary arrangements with verifying agencies so that the purpose for which an e-PRC or S-PRC is verified is recorded in the portal. Duplicate issue has been withdrawn.

quiz.question: Under the e-PRC guidelines, what must Authorized Dealers do about their staff?
options: Acquaint or train relevant head office and branch staff to issue and verify e-PRCs and S-PRCs
Train only head office IT staff, since issuance is automated
Leave training to the verifying agencies
Train staff only when a customer complains
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 12 of the guidelines asks dealers to acquaint or train relevant staff at head office and branches on issuing and verifying e-PRCs and S-PRCs, so they can guide and educate customers.

quiz.question: A remitter abroad sends money for his sister, who banks with Bank B, through Bank A in Pakistan. Which statement is correct?
options: Bank A reports the inflow and issues the e-PRC to the sister
Bank B reports the inflow and Bank A issues the e-PRC
Bank A reports the inflow in ITRS; Bank B issues the e-PRC to the sister
Both banks report the inflow and both issue an e-PRC
quiz.explanation: In the different bank model the recipient bank (Bank A) sends the money with full data to the beneficiary's bank (Bank B), which issues the e-PRC and S-PRC. Only the recipient bank reports the inflow in ITRS.

sessions.title: Branchless Banking: Agents, Account Levels and Home Remittance Accounts
sessions.summary: Run branchless banking within SBP's Branchless Banking Regulations: the bank-led model, what agents may and may not do, Level 0 and Level 1 accounts and their limits, the Home Remittance Account and the bank's duties to choose, check, supply and train the agents who serve it.
objectives: Explain the bank-led model and why the bank stays responsible for its agents' acts
Distinguish Level 0 and Level 1 branchless banking accounts by verification and limits
State what agents may do in account opening and what only the bank may do
Apply the Home Remittance Account rules and the bank's duties for agent due diligence, liquidity and training

cards.title: Behind the counter in Mardan
cards.setting: Shakeel's mobile and grocery shop, a Hingol Bank branchless banking agent, Mardan. 5:00 pm.

lines.text: Imran sahib, business is good! People open wallets here every day. I keep a copy of each CNIC in this file, just in case the bank asks.
Shakeel, that file is a problem. And who opened this account?
My neighbour's mother. She can't come in, so he gave me her details and I filled it all in for her.
Next month we launch Home Remittance Accounts here. Customers from the Gulf corridor will draw cash at your counter.
Then I'll need more cash in the drawer. And I'll be honest: I don't know the rules.
That's why we're here. Training Lead, welcome to the Agent's Shop.

scenes.heading: Only bank-led
scenes.narration: SBP's Branchless Banking Regulations allow only the bank-led model. The authorized financial institution leads the whole programme and carries all its responsibilities.

scenes.heading: Agency or joint venture
scenes.narration: A bank can work through agency arrangements or a joint venture with a telecom or other non-bank partner, in one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many set-ups.

scenes.heading: Every transaction hits a real account
scenes.narration: The customer relationship always sits with a bank. Each transaction posts to the customer's actual account, and no money is stored on the phone or a provider's server; balances there only mirror the account.

scenes.heading: Agents serve, banks decide
scenes.narration: An agent provides basic banking services on the bank's behalf under an agency agreement. The bank remains ultimately responsible, and customer contracts must say the bank answers for the agent's acts and omissions.

scenes.heading: Capacity building
scenes.narration: Section 9(b) asks banks to build their agents' capacity through training, especially on money laundering and terrorist financing risks and their implications.

cards.title: Level 0 versus Level 1 accounts
cards.caption: Section 4.3. Limits apply separately to payments and receipts. A Level 0 account moves to Level 1 after biometric verification at the customer's request.

items.label: Before biometrics
items.left: No account-to-person transfers, cash in or cash out

items.label: Daily limit
items.right: Rs. 50,000, with exceptions for salary credits and trusted merchants

items.label: Other caps
items.left: Rs. 200,000 a year and a Rs. 200,000 maximum balance
items.right: No yearly or balance cap in the table

items.label: Both levels
items.left: Screen name and CNIC against proscribed and designated lists
items.right: Call-back or OTP for remote opening

cards.question: A Level 0 customer who has not yet had biometric verification asks an agent to withdraw cash. What is the rule?
options: Allowed up to Rs. 25,000 a day
Not allowed until the customer is biometrically verified
Allowed if the agent knows the customer personally
Allowed if the customer shows a CNIC copy
cards.explanation: Section 4.3 says Level 0 account holders cannot make account-to-person transfers, cash in or cash out until their biometric verification. The daily limit applies only once those transactions are possible.

cards.title: What agents may and may not do
cards.body:
**Agents may**
- Offer basic services on the bank's behalf under a valid agency agreement: cash in, cash out, bill payments and help with account opening.
- Help customers forward their information to the bank through the electronic channel.

**Agents may not**
- Perform any element of customer due diligence: identifying the customer or beneficial owner, or understanding the nature of business. The bank does all CDD at its end.
- Keep customers' data or documents. The bank must ensure no agent retains them.
- Open accounts on behalf of other people, or let anyone operate an account for the holder.

**The bank must**
- Verify identity with NADRA, screen against proscribed and designated lists, check the data received and send the customer an opening confirmation.
- Onboard and monitor agents under SBP's 2016 agent acquisition and management framework; agent accounts are full KYC accounts.
- Keep CDD and account records for at least ten years after the relationship ends.

cards.title: Agent, bank, or nobody?
cards.prompt: Sort each task: something an agent may do, something only the bank does, or something nobody may do.

items.text: Accept a cash deposit into a customer's account
Help the customer send her details to the bank electronically
Verify the customer's identity with NADRA
Screen the name and CNIC against proscribed lists
Send the customer an account opening confirmation
Keep photocopies of customers' CNICs in a shop file
Open an account for a neighbour's mother who is not present
Let a son operate his father's account for him

cards.title: The Home Remittance Account in numbers
cards.caption: Branchless Banking Regulations, Annexure A and section 4. Credits to an HRA can come only from home remittances.

items.label: Maximum balance
items.detail: Inward home remittances have no daily limit, subject to this balance cap.

items.label: Cash withdrawal a month
items.detail: Total monthly cash withdrawal limit from the HRA.

items.label: HRA per CNIC per bank
items.detail: Individuals only, singly, Pakistani nationals.

items.label: Record retention
items.detail: Branchless banking CDD and transaction records kept at least this long.

cards.title: Launch week problems
cards.setting: Hingol Bank agent network office, Hyderabad. Monday.

lines.text: Forty agents want to offer HRAs. Twelve have no biometric device, eight ran out of cash twice last month, and three have audit findings we never closed.
And training? Annexure A says the bank must make sure agents are properly trained to serve HRA customers.
I have a biometric device and a good cash position now. I'd like to offer home delivery too, for elderly customers.
Home delivery carries a risk of misappropriation. The Regulations want extra controls if we do it.
So, Training Lead: which agents go live, and what has to happen first?

cards.title: Choosing agents for the HRA launch
cards.situation: Hingol Bank's business team wants all 40 interested agents live with Home Remittance Accounts next week, including those with no biometric device, recent cash shortages or open audit findings. Training is planned 'after launch'.

choices.text: Go live only at agents with biometric devices that pass enhanced due diligence, have liquidity reassessed, sign revised service agreements and finish HRA training; bring the others in as they qualify.
choices.outcome: Right. Annexure A paragraph 17 limits HRA opening and transactions to agent locations with biometric devices, and requires enhanced due diligence with ongoing monitoring and periodic audit, a liquidity reassessment, revised agreements where needed and properly trained agents.

choices.text: Launch all 40 now and train them during the first month, since volumes will be low.
choices.outcome: Poor. HRA services are allowed only where biometric devices exist, and agents must be properly trained to serve customers. Launching first and training later breaks both.

choices.text: Launch at the 28 agents with biometric devices and check due diligence and cash later.
choices.outcome: Partly right. The biometric condition is met, but enhanced due diligence, liquidity reassessment and training are conditions of serving HRAs, not follow-ups.

choices.text: Delay the launch until every one of the 40 agents qualifies.
choices.outcome: Partly right on caution, but unnecessary. Qualified agents can serve customers now while others catch up, which supports the scheme's inclusion goal.

cards.title: The bank's duties for HRAs and agents
cards.prompt: Match each item from Annexure A, paragraph 17 to what it requires.

pairs.right: Open HRAs and run their transactions only where agents have biometric devices
Enhanced due diligence of interested agents, ongoing monitoring and periodic audit
Reassess each agent's cash capacity and keep cash available
Protect customers' financial and non-financial data from leakage and misuse
Ensure agents are properly trained to serve HRA customers
No service charges when an HRA is opened or closed

cards.title: Opening an HRA at an agent
cards.prompt: Put the steps for opening a Home Remittance Account at an agent in order.
steps: Customer visits an agent location that has a biometric device
Agent captures the customer's details and biometrics and forwards them electronically to the bank
Bank verifies identity through NADRA biometric verification, at no cost to the customer
Bank screens the name and CNIC against proscribed and designated lists and completes CDD
Bank activates the account instantly and sends the customer confirmation; the agent keeps no data

cards.title: HRA and agent rules worth remembering

cards.back: Only home remittances may be credited to it.
Not permitted from branchless banking accounts at all.
One-time registration with expected senders and countries; a remote registrant visits an agent once before any debit.
Extra controls and monitoring, real-time SMS alerts on amounts and charges, and a separate MIS of such withdrawals.
Published every calendar quarter at branches, agent locations and the website; not raised during the quarter.
Received 24 hours by SMS, IVR and email, acknowledged with a unique number and an estimated time to resolve.

cards.question: A customer wants a cousin in Karachi to transfer rupees into her Home Remittance Account so she can withdraw it at Shakeel's shop. What should Shakeel tell her?
options: That is fine, any domestic transfer can credit an HRA
Only home remittances can be credited to an HRA
Domestic credits are allowed up to Rs. 50,000 a day
She must first upgrade the HRA to Level 0
cards.explanation: Annexure A says credit in an HRA can only be made through home remittances, and paragraph 17(g) asks banks to ensure HRAs are fed with home remittance proceeds. A domestic transfer would need a different account.

cards.title: Training agents that actually works
cards.body:
Two provisions make agent training a duty: **section 9(b)** (capacity building, especially on ML/TF risks) and **Annexure A, paragraph 17(f)** (agents properly trained to serve HRA customers).

- Teach the **don'ts** first: no CDD, no copies, no accounts for absent people.
- Use the agent's own counter: what a suspicious cash-out looks like, how to refuse politely, who to call.
- Cover fraud and PIN safety, because agents also educate first-time customers.
- Check understanding at refresher visits, not just at onboarding.

cards.title: Agent's Shop take-aways
items: Only the bank-led model is allowed; the bank is responsible for its agents and every transaction posts to a real account.
Agents may help customers forward information but never perform CDD, keep customer data or open accounts for absent people.
Level 0 needs NADRA verification and cannot cash in, cash out or send to persons before biometrics; Level 1 needs biometrics and has higher limits.
HRAs are Level 1 sub-accounts fed only by home remittances, with a PKR 1.5m balance cap and PKR 500,000 monthly cash withdrawal.
HRA agents need biometric devices, enhanced due diligence, monitoring, audit, enough cash and proper training.

cards.prompt: If you visited one of your bank's agents tomorrow, which single habit would you check first, and what would you say if you found a file of customer CNIC copies?

quiz.question: Which branchless banking model do SBP's Branchless Banking Regulations allow?
options: Only the bank-led model
Only the telecom-led model
Bank-led or telecom-led, at the bank's choice
Any model the agent prefers
quiz.explanation: Section 3 of the Regulations allows only the bank-led model, in which the financial institution leads the programme and carries its responsibilities, whether through agency arrangements or a joint venture.

quiz.question: An agent offers to verify a new customer's identity and assess the nature of his business so the bank can save time. What do the Regulations say?
options: Agents may verify identity but not assess the business
Agents may not perform any element of CDD; the bank does all CDD at its end
Agents may perform full CDD if they hold a bank account and have signed an agency agreement
Agents may perform CDD for Level 0 accounts only
quiz.explanation: Section 4.2(b)(ix) bars agents from performing CDD elements, including identifying the customer or beneficial owner and understanding the nature of business. Their role is limited to helping customers forward information electronically.

quiz.question: What is the daily transaction limit on a Level 1 branchless banking account under section 4.3?
options: Rs. 25,000, with no exceptions at all
Rs. 200,000, the same as the monthly limit, so that salaried customers are never restricted
Rs. 50,000, with exceptions for employer salary credits and trusted merchants
Rs. 1,500,000, the same as an HRA balance
quiz.explanation: Section 4.3 sets Level 1 at Rs. 50,000 per day and Rs. 200,000 per month. The daily limit does not apply to salary credits from employers against proof of employment or to payments to trusted merchants such as schools and hospitals.

quiz.question: Shakeel keeps photocopies of customers' CNICs in a file at his shop 'in case the bank asks'. What does section 4.3 require of the bank?
options: Ensure the agent locks the file in a safe
Ensure that no customer data or documents are retained by the agent
Ensure the agent destroys copies after one year
Ensure the agent shares copies with the bank monthly
quiz.explanation: Among the bank's responsibilities in section 4.3 is ensuring that no customer's data and documents are retained by the agent. Locking or later destroying the copies does not meet that duty.

quiz.question: What is the maximum balance of a Home Remittance Account?
options: No maximum balance at all
quiz.explanation: Annexure A sets no daily limit on inward home remittances but caps the HRA balance at PKR 1,500,000. PKR 500,000 is the monthly cash withdrawal limit, and PKR 200,000 is a Level 0 cap.

quiz.question: Hingol Bank wants to offer HRA services at an agent who has no biometric device but an excellent compliance record. What does Annexure A allow?
options: HRA services at any agent with a clean audit report
HRA transactions, but not account opening, at that agent
HRA services at that agent, provided the agent calls the bank to confirm each customer's identity
HRA opening and transactions only at agent locations with biometric devices
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 17(a) allows opening HRAs and related transactions only at agent locations where biometric devices are available. A good record does not replace that condition.

quiz.question: Before serving HRA customers, which due diligence must Hingol Bank conduct on interested agents?
options: Simplified due diligence, since agents are low risk
A one-time check at onboarding, with no later review
Enhanced due diligence, with ongoing monitoring and periodic audit
Only a credit check on the agent's business
quiz.explanation: Annexure A paragraph 17(c) requires enhanced due diligence of interested agents and continued effective ongoing monitoring, including periodic audit.

quiz.question: A Hingol customer abroad asks to send money out of Pakistan from his branchless banking wallet to pay a supplier in Dubai. What is the rule?
options: Permitted from Level 1 accounts up to the daily limit
Permitted only through an agent with a biometric device
Cross-border outward remittances from branchless banking accounts are not permitted
Permitted if the customer completes Form M at the agent and the agent forwards it to the bank
quiz.explanation: Section 5(b) of the Regulations says banks shall not permit cross-border outward remittance transactions from branchless banking accounts. The limits and forms in the other options do not create an exception.

quiz.question: Hingol wants to add home delivery of remittance cash for elderly HRA customers. Which control set do the Regulations require?
options: A signed waiver from each customer accepting any loss in delivery, which removes the need for alerts
Delivery only by the customer's relatives, with no SMS alerts
Additional controls and monitoring, real-time SMS alerts and a separate MIS of such withdrawals
No extra controls, because the cash comes from the same HRA
quiz.explanation: Annexure A paragraph 18 requires additional controls and monitoring for home delivery given the misappropriation risk, real-time SMS on amounts received, withdrawn and charged, and a separate MIS for quick complaint resolution.

quiz.question: Which provision of the Branchless Banking Regulations asks banks to build agents' capacity through training, especially on ML/TF risks?
options: Section 4.4
Section 6.4
Annexure B
Section 9(b)
quiz.explanation: Section 9(b) requires adequate measures for agents' capacity building through trainings, especially on ML/TF risks and their implications. Section 4.4 covers domestic fund transfers, section 6.4 internal audit, and Annexure B customer awareness.

sessions.title: Wire Transfer Information, the FX Training Programme and Inspection Readiness
sessions.summary: Keep the right originator and beneficiary information with every wire and home remittance under SBP's AML/CFT/CPF Regulations and the Branchless Banking Regulations, then build the board-approved foreign exchange training programme Chapter 2 requires, with its annual needs assessment, and show an SBP inspector the roles, records and evidence behind it.
objectives: Describe, in general terms, the duties of ordering, intermediary and beneficiary institutions for wire transfer information
Apply the Branchless Banking Regulations' information rules for home remittances above and below USD 1,000
Build an FX training programme that meets the seven parameters of Chapter 2, paragraph 3
Assemble the roles, records and training evidence an SBP review of FX, remittance and branchless banking work will ask for

cards.title: Ten days to inspection
cards.setting: Board Risk Committee room, Hingol Bank head office, Karachi. 4:00 pm.

lines.text: SBP's inspection team arrives in ten days. Two items are on my desk: an inbound SWIFT payment with no originator address or ID, and the board paper on our FX training policy.
Trade sees the same thing. Payments arrive with a name and nothing else, and the business wants them credited today.
And my home remittance files: do we really keep originator details for every small remittance?
Gulberg has finished its training-needs assessments. Every FX officer, plus our two call-centre colleagues.
Good. Training Lead, this is the final stage: get the information right on every transfer, then show the board a training programme SBP would accept.

cards.title: Who carries the information in a wire

scenes.heading: The ordering institution
scenes.narration: The bank sending a wire identifies and verifies its originator, and records enough detail to reconstruct the transfer: date, currency and amount, value date, purpose, beneficiary and beneficiary institution, and the relationship between the parties where relevant.

scenes.heading: Information that travels
scenes.narration: The payment message carries the originator's name, account number or unique reference, and identity document number, and the beneficiary's name and identity document number, all the way along the chain.

scenes.heading: The intermediary
scenes.narration: A bank in the middle passes all of that information on, keeps a record of what it received, and takes reasonable steps, consistent with straight-through processing, to spot cross-border wires with missing information.

scenes.heading: The beneficiary institution
scenes.narration: The receiving bank verifies the beneficiary if not already done, and uses risk-based policies to handle wires that arrive incomplete, including whether to execute, suspend or reject, and whether to report to the FMU.

scenes.heading: Weak counterparts
scenes.narration: Banks limit or prohibit relationships and transactions with institutions that do not meet wire transfer standards.

cards.title: What must travel with a wire (Regulation 11)
cards.caption: SBP AML/CFT/CPF Regulations, Regulation 11(3), in general terms. Batch files from one originator must also carry traceable beneficiary information.

items.label: Originator's name
items.detail: Who is sending the money.

items.label: Originator's account or unique reference
items.detail: Lets the transfer be traced end to end.

items.label: Originator's identity document number
items.detail: The applicable ID document number.

items.label: Beneficiary's name
items.detail: Who should receive the money.

items.label: Beneficiary's identity document number
items.detail: The applicable ID document number.

cards.title: Whose duty is it?
cards.prompt: Sort each wire transfer duty to the institution that carries it under Regulation 11.

items.text: Identify and verify the originator before sending
Record purpose and relationship details so the wire can be reconstructed
Pass on all originator and beneficiary data unchanged
Keep a record of all information received from the previous bank
Spot cross-border wires lacking information, consistent with straight-through processing
Verify the beneficiary's identity if not already verified
Weigh incomplete information when deciding to execute or report to the FMU

cards.question: An inbound cross-border payment for a Hingol customer arrives with the originator's name only. What does Regulation 11 expect of Hingol as beneficiary institution?
options: Credit it at once, since the beneficiary is a known customer
Return it automatically, since any gap means rejection
Apply its risk-based policy, treating the gap as a factor in executing it and in judging suspicion
Ask the customer to supply the missing originator details and credit on his word
cards.explanation: Regulation 11(6) requires risk-based policies, procedures and controls for incoming wires lacking complete information. The gap may be a factor in deciding whether to execute or terminate and whether the transaction is suspicious and merits reporting to the FMU.

cards.title: Home remittances through branchless banking: information rules
cards.body:
Section 5 of the Branchless Banking Regulations adds rules for home remittances into branchless banking accounts.

**USD 1,000 or more** must carry the originator's name, account number (or unique reference), and the originator's address, national identity number, customer identification number, or date and place of birth; plus the beneficiary's name and account number or unique reference.

**Below USD 1,000** must carry the originator's name and account number or unique reference, and the beneficiary's name and account number or unique reference. This information need not be verified for accuracy unless there is a suspicion of ML/TF.

**Also**
- Batch files from one originator must contain accurate originator data and traceable beneficiary data.
- Intermediaries in Pakistan keep the information for at least ten years.
- Banks use reasonable measures, including post-event or real-time monitoring, to spot remittances with missing data, and set risk-based policies on when to execute, reject or suspend.

cards.title: Home remittances: above and below USD 1,000

items.label: Originator
items.left: Name, account or unique reference, plus address, ID number, customer number, or date and place of birth
items.right: Name and account number or unique reference

items.label: Beneficiary
items.left: Name and account number or unique reference
items.right: Name and account number or unique reference

items.label: Verification
items.left: As for the bank's own customer and on suspicion
items.right: Not required unless ML/TF is suspected

items.label: Records
items.left: Intermediary keeps the data at least ten years
items.right: Intermediary keeps the data at least ten years

cards.title: The board asks for the training policy
cards.setting: Board Risk Committee, Hingol Bank. The following morning.

lines.text: The committee wants to know if our FX training meets Chapter 2, paragraph 3. Over to you, Training Lead.
My worry: our trade staff get AML training from compliance and FX training from treasury, and the two never meet.
Mine: remote branches. Our officer in Chitral has had no FX course in two years.
And finance has proposed cutting classroom training to one e-learning module a year for everyone. Let's hear your plan.

cards.title: The yearly FX training cycle
cards.caption: Chapter 2, paragraph 3 of the Foreign Exchange Manual, read as one cycle.

items.label: Board-approved policy
items.detail: Covers all major FX areas and how staff are selected for programmes.

items.label: Needs assessment each January
items.detail: Every related employee assessed at the start of the calendar year.

items.label: Risk-based focus areas
items.detail: Trade, FC accounts, remittances, investments, set before the year starts.

items.label: Modules with AML/CFT and IT built in
items.detail: AML/CFT, e-commerce and IT operations are integral parts.

items.label: Delivery for all, remote too
items.detail: Plans for remote branches; in-house trainers; IBP, NIBAF and universities.

items.label: Assess and reward
items.detail: Post-training assessment; FX training counts towards career growth.

cards.title: The one-module proposal
cards.situation: Finance proposes replacing Hingol Bank's FX training with a single annual e-learning module for all FX staff, dropping separate plans for remote branches and the post-training assessment, to cut costs.

choices.text: Keep a board-approved, needs-based programme: assess each employee in January, keep remote-branch plans and post-training assessment, and use in-house trainers and e-learning to cut cost.
choices.outcome: Right. Paragraph 3 expects a board-approved policy, a yearly needs assessment per employee, plans for remote branches at par with urban ones and a mechanism to assess staff after training. Cheaper delivery is fine; dropping these elements is not.

choices.text: Accept the proposal, since any training at all satisfies the Manual.
choices.outcome: Poor. A single module for everyone ignores the individual needs assessment, risk-based focus areas, remote-branch plans and post-training assessment that paragraph 3 sets out.

choices.text: Accept it for urban branches but keep classroom training for remote branches.
choices.outcome: Partly right. It protects remote staff, but still drops individual needs assessment and post-training assessment for everyone else.

choices.text: Reject any change and keep all classroom training exactly as it is.
choices.outcome: Partly right. The duties are protected, but paragraph 3 encourages in-house trainers and tailored courses; smarter delivery can cut cost without losing compliance.

cards.title: Paragraph 3, one parameter at a time
cards.prompt: Match each parameter of Chapter 2, paragraph 3 to what it asks of the Authorized Dealer.

pairs.right: Assess each related employee's FX training needs at the start of each calendar year
Pick risk-based focus areas such as trade, FC accounts and remittances before the year starts
Give function-specific FX training due weight in employees' career progression
Make AML/CFT, e-commerce and IT operations integral to FX modules
Plan training so remote-branch staff build capacity at par with urban staff
Develop in-house trainers, assess staff after training, work with IBP, NIBAF and universities

cards.question: When does Chapter 2 require an Authorized Dealer to assess each related employee's foreign exchange training needs?
options: Whenever SBP announces an inspection
At the beginning of each calendar year
Only when an employee joins the FX function
Every three years, with the board's policy review
cards.explanation: Paragraph 3(i) requires the assessment, for each related employee, at the beginning of each calendar year. Induction and inspection-driven training can add to it but do not replace it.

cards.back: Sets the branchless banking strategy and policies, takes an explicit, documented decision to offer it, and ensures proper security policies.
Implements the strategy, oversees security and outsourcing risk, and widens audit and compliance coverage with skilled staff.
Ensures compliance controls are built into the system and is consulted while products are developed and implemented.
Reviews critical processes and outsourced activities on a risk basis and escalates significant exceptions to the Audit Committee.
ML/TF risk assessed before launch, with measures to manage and mitigate the risks.
Banks assess branchless banking ML/TF risks every year, in light of the national risk assessment.

cards.title: Hingol case: the 2027 FX training plan
cards.body:
A fictional case from Hingol Bank's files.

The board approved a revised FX training and development policy. In January, line managers completed a needs assessment for 214 related employees.

**What the plan covered**
- **Branch FX staff and call-centre agents:** services to individuals and outward remittance forms (Chapter 2, para 4(ii)).
- **Remittance and branch staff:** the home remittance clock, compensation and e-PRC issue and verification (Chapter 10).
- **Trade staff:** a joint FX and trade-based money laundering module, with AML/CFT built in.
- **Agent managers and agents:** CDD limits, data, HRA service and ML/TF red flags (BB Regulations s.9(b) and Annexure A).
- **Remote branches:** in-house trainers visiting Chitral, Turbat and Skardu.

Every course ended with an assessment, and results fed into appraisals. The inspector asked for three things: the board approval, the January assessments and the test results. All three were ready.

cards.title: Inspection Room take-aways
items: Wires carry originator and beneficiary names, account or reference numbers and ID numbers through the whole payment chain.
Beneficiary banks use risk-based policies for incomplete wires; the gap can affect execution and STR decisions.
Home remittances of USD 1,000 or more need fuller originator data; intermediaries keep it for at least ten years.
Chapter 2, paragraph 3 needs a board-approved FX training policy and a needs assessment for each related employee every January.
Build in AML/CFT and IT topics, plan for remote branches, assess staff after training and keep the evidence for SBP.

cards.prompt: If an SBP inspector asked you tomorrow for proof that your FX or remittance staff are trained for their roles, what three documents would you hand over, and which one is missing today?

quiz.question: Under Regulation 11, which item must travel with a wire transfer through the payment chain?
options: The originator's salary slip
The beneficiary's credit score
The originator's identity document number
The originator's tax return
quiz.explanation: Regulation 11(3) lists the originator's name, account number or unique reference and identity document number, and the beneficiary's name and identity document number. The other items are not wire transfer information.

quiz.question: Hingol Bank acts as an intermediary in a cross-border payment chain. Which duty applies to it under Regulation 11?
options: Verify the identity of the final beneficiary in person before passing the payment on to the next bank
Keep all originator and beneficiary information with the wire and keep a record of it
Verify the originator's identity documents personally
Delete the information once the payment is passed on
quiz.explanation: Regulation 11(9) requires an intermediary to maintain all required information with the wire, keep a record of what it receives, take STP-consistent measures to spot gaps and have risk-based policies on execution. Verifying the parties falls to the ordering and beneficiary institutions.

quiz.question: A home remittance of USD 1,500 to a branchless banking account arrives with only the originator's name and account number. What is missing under section 5 of the Branchless Banking Regulations?
options: Nothing, because the originator's name and account number are always enough for any home remittance
The beneficiary's employer and monthly income
The purpose of remittance certified by an embassy
Originator's address, national ID, customer ID, or date and place of birth
quiz.explanation: For home remittances of USD 1,000 or more, section 5(c) adds the originator's address, national identity number, customer identification number, or date and place of birth to the name and account number or unique reference.

quiz.question: For a home remittance below USD 1,000, when must the bank verify the accuracy of the accompanying originator information?
options: Only where there is a suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing
Always, before crediting the beneficiary
Never, even if ML/TF is suspected
Only if the remittance comes from a country the bank has not seen before for that beneficiary
quiz.explanation: Section 5(e) says information on remittances below USD 1,000 need not be verified for accuracy, but the bank must verify its customer's information where ML/TF is suspected.

quiz.question: How long must an intermediary financial institution in Pakistan keep originator and beneficiary information received with a home remittance?
options: At least five years after the account is closed
At least ten years after the transaction is completed
Until the beneficiary withdraws the funds
At least one year after the transaction
quiz.explanation: Section 5(h) requires intermediary institutions within Pakistan to retain all originator and beneficiary information that accompanies a home remittance for at least ten years following completion of the transaction.

quiz.question: Who must approve an Authorized Dealer's foreign exchange training and development policy under Chapter 2, paragraph 3?
options: The board of directors
The head of human resources
The Institute of Bankers Pakistan
SBP's Exchange Policy Department
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3 asks Authorized Dealers to prepare a comprehensive training and development policy, approved by their board of directors, for all major FX areas, including how staff are selected for programmes.

quiz.question: Hingol Bank's FX training plan covers trade and remittance rules but has no AML/CFT or IT content. Which parameter of Chapter 2, paragraph 3 does it miss?
options: Coordinating with IBP and NIBAF on course design
Making AML/CFT, e-commerce and IT operations integral to FX modules
Identifying risk-based focus areas such as trade and remittances before the calendar year starts
Developing in-house trainers for internal support
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3(iv) requires dealers, when preparing FX training modules, to make function-specific training in critical areas such as AML/CFT, e-commerce and IT operations an integral part of them.

quiz.question: An FX officer at a remote branch in Chitral has received no FX training in two years, while Karachi staff train every year. Which paragraph 3 parameter addresses this?
options: Giving FX training weight in career growth
Training plans for remote-area staff so their capacity is at par with urban centres
Choosing training focus areas by risk
Assessing employees' performance after training
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3(v) asks dealers to develop training plans for employees posted at branches in remote areas so their capacity building is at par with staff in urban centres.

quiz.question: Under the Branchless Banking Regulations, to whom does internal audit escalate significant exceptions found in branchless banking?
options: The agent network manager
The Financial Monitoring Unit
The telecom partner's board
The Audit Committee of the board
quiz.explanation: Section 6.4(d) requires internal audit to escalate significant exceptions to the Audit Committee of the board, after risk-based reviews of critical processes and outsourced activities.

quiz.question: Which is the best evidence that Hingol Bank met Chapter 2, paragraph 3(i) this year?
options: Records of each related employee's FX training-needs assessment made at the start of the year
A list of all FX courses offered by the training department during the year, with their dates and venues
The total training budget approved for the year
Attendance at last year's SBP outreach session
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3(i) is about assessing each related employee's FX training needs at the beginning of each calendar year. Only individual assessment records show that; course lists and budgets do not.
